Pathological evidence of
encephalomyelitis in the
stiff man syndrome with
anti-GAD antibodies
Jason D. Warren1 B MED SCI MB BS (HONS), Grace Scott2
FRACPATH, Peter C. Blumbergs1,2 MB BS FRACPATH,
Philip D. Thompson1 MB PHD FRACP
1Department of Neurology, Royal Adelaide Hospital, and
University Department of Medicine, University of Adelaide,
2Department of Neuropathology, Institute of Medical and
Veterinary Science Adelaide, South Australia
Summary We report the case of a 57 year old woman with typical
clinical features of the stiff man syndrome (SMS) and antibodies to
glutamic acid decarboxylase (antiGADAb), who developed a supra-
nuclear gaze palsy, ileus and died of bronchopneumonia eight
years after the onset of illness. Post mortem examination revealed
perivascular lymphocyte cuffing throughout the cerebral hemis-
pheres, brainstem and spinal cord and neuronal loss in medial
anterior horns of the cervical spinal cord. These findings support
the notion that the SMS and progressive encephalomyelitis
with rigidity (PER) form a clinical and pathologic continuum. & 2002

CASE REPORT
A 57 year old woman presented with a three year history of
gradually progressive stiffness of the legs, difficulty walking
and painful spontaneous extensor spasms of the legs. The
spasms destabilised walking leading to falls. There was no
weakness, sensory loss, sphincteric disturbance or visual
symptoms. A diagnosis of SMS was made. 1 There was no past
history of diabetes mellitus, other endocrine disease or sig-
nificant illness and no family history of neurological disease.
When first examined, cognitive functions, the cranial nerves
and upper limbs were normal. The lower limbs were held in a
rigidly extended posture. Attempts to move the legs caused
muscular spasms and pain. There was no clonus, and power, as
could be assessed, was normal. Tendon reflexes were normal
and plantar responses were flexor. Sensory examination and
coordination were normal. Gait was severely impaired by lower
limb spasms. Extensive investigations including biochemical
and haematological screens, brain and spinal cord imaging,
and cerebrospinal fluid examination were normal. Thyroid and
adrenal function was normal. Gastric parietal, pancreatic
islet cell and thyroid microsomal antibodies were present.
Antibodies to GAD were detected in plasma and cerebrospinal
fluid.
2 Electromyography of the lower limbs demonstrated
continuous motor unit activity, comprising units of normal

morphology, despite attempted relaxation. Peripheral nerve
conduction was normal.
Baclofen, diazepam and vigabatrin produced some impro-
vement in spasms and mobility but this was not sustained. A
single dose of intrathecal baclofen produced a prolonged con-
fusional state. Trials of plasmapharesis, prednisolone and aza-
thioprine were undertaken without improvement. Increasing
falls over the next four years were associated with fractures and
declining mobility requiring nursing home care.
Five years after the illness began, the patient developed ileus
and a bacterial overgrowth syndrome. Three years later, a pro-
longed episode of ileus was complicated by metabolic acidosis
and delirium. There was no evidence of diabetes mellitus. Spa-
sms continued, and were accompanied by generalised muscular
rigidity, a fine tremor of extremities, extensor posturing and
profuse sweating. There was a supranuclear paresis of vertical
(predominantly downward) gaze, brisk flexor withdrawal
reflexes of both legs, and rigidity of the abdominal wall and
erector spinae muscles. Her condition deteriorated, and she
developed bronchopneumonia as a terminal event eight years
after the onset of illness.
At post mortem, the brain (weight 1180 grams) and spinal
cord were macroscopically normal. Microscopically, there was
mild perivascular lymphocytic cuffing throughout the brain,
brainstem and meninges. Sparse perivascular cuffing by pre-
dominantly T lymphocytes (UCHL-1 and CD45Ro immuno-
positive) was present throughout the spinal cord (Fig. 1),
predominantly in the grey matter. There was subtotal loss of

medial anterior horn cells in the cervical and lumbosacral cord
but lateral large motor neurones were preserved (Fig. 2). There
were no signs of demyelination in the cerebral hemispheres,
brainstem or spinal cord. There was also diffuse T cell lym-
phocyte infiltration of the thyroid consistent with autoimmune
thyroiditis.
DISCUSSION
This patient presented with typical clinical features of the SMS 1
with antiGADAb, 2 but the illness progressed relentlessly over
eight years and a supranuclear gaze paresis developed. This
development and the post mortem finding of extensive, peri-
vascular lymphocyte cuffing at multiple levels throughout the
central nervous system is typical of PER. The patient was
included in the original report of Solimena et al., 2 in which
antibodies against gamma-aminobutyric-acid (GABA)-ergic
neurones were demonstrated in the serum and cerebrospinal
fluid in 60% of patients with a clinical diagnosis of stiff man
syndrome. These observations prompted the suggestion of an
autoimmune aetiology for SMS. 2,3
Pathological examination of the central nervous system in
patients with the SMS has yielded various findings. These have
included normal or subtle change of uncertain significance, 1,4–7
loss of anterior horn cells and spinal interneurones 8–13 and
lymphocytic cuffing around brainstem and spinal cord
meningeal vessels. 11,12 In the six pathological studies of SMS
with antiGADAb, perivascular lymphocytic cuffing was evi-
dent in three (present case
11), vacuolar degeneration of anterior
horn cells was found in one 13 and in three, there was neuronal
loss in the spinal cord (present case 14,15).
The finding of encephalomyelitis, perivascular lymphocyte
cuffing, loss of small and medium-sized ventral horn neurones,
and demyelination sparing corticospinal tracts, in patients with
axial rigidity and spasms, has been described previously as
progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
(PER).
16–19 Two recent series of SMS included examples of
PER.12,20 These were distinguished from SMS by additional
extrapyramidal, brainstem, long tract and lower motor neurone
signs and a cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis, and a progressive
course, in contrast to the more indolent course of SMS.
The antiGADAb status of most pathologically proven PER
is not known, nor was it known in two cases of SMS with
pathological evidence of encephalomyelitis. 10,12 The present
case is the third reported instance of an illness beginning as
typical SMS with anti-GAD antibodies in which encephalo-
myelitis was subsequently found. The disease duration in these
cases ranged from six to eight years, longer than most reported
cases of PER. The late evolution of ocular motor signs in two
of these cases suggests a change in the clinical picture from
SMS to PER. These observations raise the question of whe-
ther there is clinical and pathological overlap between PER
and SMS, and whether these conditions form a continuum
of encephalomyelopathies, rather than representing distinct
entities.
